en: Therīgāthā 13.1 Vīsatinipāta:
The Verses of the Elder Nun Ambapālī
"My hair on the head was black,
resembling the color of bees, with curled tips;
through old age, it became like coarse hemp."
The word of the speaker of truth is not otherwise.
Like a fragrant casket scented with perfume,
my head-born son is filled with flowers.
That word of the speaker of truth, which is unfailing, grows like a fragrant lotus with its hair-like filaments;
it is like a well-tended grove planted by the wise.
Adorned with the variegated tips of hairpins and combs,
that [head] is now sparse here and there due to old age— just so,
the word of one who speaks truth is never otherwise.
Adorned with black locks and decorated with gold,
it shone when fashioned into a beautiful braid;
yet now, by old age, that head has been made to falter.
The word of the speaker of truth is not otherwise.
Just like a drawing well-executed by a painter,
those beautiful eyebrows of mine used to adorn my face in the past.
Hanging down with folds of skin due to old age,
yet [remaining] true to the word of the Speaker of Truth;
radiant and beautiful like a gem.
They were once deep blue and long; now,
struck down by old age, they no longer shine—
truly, the word of the Speaker of Truth is never otherwise.
Her nose, like a delicate peak,
shone with the beauty of her early youth; yet,
as if overwhelmed by old age, it now appears as though it were being eroded.
The word of the speaker of truth is not otherwise.
Like a well-fashioned, well-finished bracelet,
may it adorn my ears.
Hanging down with folds of skin due to old age,
they resemble the color of a cluster of *pattalī* flowers; such is the word of the Speaker of Truth, never otherwise.
O Sobhara, those teeth of mine were once beautiful and even;
now they are broken and blackened by old age—
thus the word of the Speaker of Truth is not otherwise.
Like a cuckoo wandering through the forest thickets in the woods, warbling sweetly,
she stumbles here and there because of old age.
The word of one who speaks truth is not otherwise.
My neck shone beautifully in the past, like a well-polished conch shell.
She was broken and bent by old age;
the word of the Speaker of Truth is not otherwise.
Both are like the comparison of a crossbar in a wheel-rim.
O Sobhari, those beautiful arms of mine were once firm;
now they are withered by old age like the bark of a *pāṭali* tree.
The word of the speaker of truth is not otherwise.
Those hands of mine in the past, adorned with delicate rings and gold, shone so brightly; now,
through old age, they are like roots and rootless plants.
The word of the speaker of truth is not otherwise.
Those two breasts of mine, once plump, rounded, firm,
and uplifted, used to adorn my chest.
Like a well-polished golden plate,
the word of one who speaks truth does not hang loose like water from a sieve; it is never otherwise.
My body once shone brightly in the past;
now it is covered with fine wrinkles— truly,
the word of the speaker of truth is not otherwise.
Those two thighs of mine in the past,
which were as beautiful as the coils of a serpent,
have now become like bamboo canes through old age.
The word of the speaker of truth is never otherwise.
Those shanks of mine in the past, adorned with delicate anklets and gold, were truly beautiful.
Like sesame stalks withered by age,
the word of the Speaker of Truth is never otherwise;
both are like the simile of cotton filled with fluff.
O Sobhari, my feet were once beautiful;
now they are cracked and wrinkled by old age— just so,
for the word of the Speaker of Truth is never otherwise.
Thus indeed is this physical aggregate:
flickering, a repository of many sufferings,
fallen into defilement, a house of old age.
“The word of the speaker of truth is not otherwise.
… [Thus spoke] the Elder Nun Ambapālī.
